prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength bring the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my preferred single part, but after the first round I hold it with less margin than before. The case rests on three things that the discussion did not dislodge. First, the magic-wavelength lattice is a specific idea that lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be interrogated with the trapping light-shift cancelled, and that is what distinguishes it from the single-ion clocks and from the comb. Second, the resulting uncertainty and stability near 10^-18 has been reached and compared by several independent laboratories, so no part of the result rests on a single group's claim. Third, the credit is two names with an idea-plus-realisation split that no member has disputed. In answer to the chair's question about new physics and not only new accuracy: what I can state with confidence is that the clocks turned the lattice into a controllable many-body system, so that atom-atom interactions and collective effects became a limiting systematic and a thing to be studied, and that clock comparisons now probe relativity and the constancy of constants at a level that was not accessible before. I recall differential gravitational-redshift measurements across millimetre to centimetre scales within one lattice, but I have not checked those results or their dates against a supplied source, and the committee should treat that point as recollection. I also accept Olsson's and Lindroth's shared observation that the redefinition of the second is a future event and carries no weight as evidence of merit in my case.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections remain the ones I listed in round 1, and the second round has sharpened rather than removed them. A clock is an instrument and, for several colleagues, the discovery content is thin compared with a prediction confirmed by nature; I think that overstates the difference but I cannot show that the new physics is as large as in a new phase of matter. The 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes cover much of the enabling toolbox, ion clocks reach comparable uncertainties, and a citation that does not say what is specific to lattices would read as a verdict between ions and lattices, which I do not want. Credit is not complete, since Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the other lattice groups are outside the two names, and I have not verified the priority details. Finally, my own Hall-laboratory link means that my vote on this candidate must be discounted, and a configuration whose only two supporters are an atomic physicist with a Boulder connection and a relativistic-atomic-structure theorist is weaker than the count suggests. Against B038 specifically, I concede that six of eight members prefer it with an identical trio and a prediction-plus-discovery structure, and that I cannot name a scientific error in that case.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B045 fifth and asks what new physics, as opposed to new accuracy, the lattice clock has revealed, and says that a redefinition of the second has not happened so timeliness cannot rest on it.
responses.response: I accept her second point without reservation and I have dropped the redefinition from my argument. On the first, the part I can defend is that the many-atom lattice made interactions and collective effects in a clock a measurable and controllable quantity, and that sub-10^-18 comparisons give tests of relativity and constants that no earlier clock allowed. That is real, but I will not claim it matches the opening of a new phase diagram, and I would not describe it as a discovery of a new state of matter. If the committee defines a discovery as a new phenomenon, her argument counts against me; if it counts a new measurement regime with new tests of nature, it does not. We differ on that criterion and not on the facts, and I leave the criterion to the vote.

responses.point: Mehlig separates the pairing mechanism from the discovery in B038, argues that the existence of the correlated and superconducting states is confirmed across many groups, and says that waiting for the mechanism would tie recognition to a question that may stay open for decades.
responses.response: This moves me more than anything else in the first round. In round 1 I treated the open mechanism as a reason to weigh B038 below the clock, but his comparison with prizes where the observation was secure long before the explanation is correct, and the sample-to-sample variation I worried about does not change the fact that independent laboratories see the same phase diagram. I therefore withdraw the claim that B038's open questions make it less ready than clocks in any sense that should decide the prize. I keep two narrower points: the experimental credit is more contestable than the clock credit, since the first author and other groups cannot be added under the three-name cap, and I would want the citation to state the observed phenomena and make no mechanism claim, which he also proposes. His answer to Danielsson, that Bistritzer and MacDonald identified the magic angle quantitatively and so are the decisive prediction, seems right to me, and I am relying on his recollection, not on a checked source.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that no precision-measurement candidate is available to pair with B045 so a single clean part is best, and that the agreement of independent clocks at 10^-18 is a physical test and not engineering alone.
responses.response: I agree that a single part is the right form, and the three-name cap makes any pairing with B038 impossible without dropping one of its credited names, so I withdraw my round-1 worry about it. I am less sure the agreement between clocks carries as much weight with those who read clocks as instruments, and I would not rest the case on that phrase alone. Where I would go beyond her is the wording: the citation should say neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, so that the prize does not read as settling the ion-versus-lattice question. We two are both atomic physicists reasoning from the same vantage point, so the committee should weigh our agreement accordingly and not count it as two independent confirmations.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from B016 to B038 after the opening ballots, anchors the citation on the 2011 prediction and the 2018 observation without a mechanism claim, and keeps B045 as a fallback if the committee wants a precision-measurement prize.
responses.response: I note the chair's change of position from B016, which he explains openly, and I respect that he flags that his reading of the priority history rests on the ballots and recollection. I disagree with one qualification: he says lattice clocks build directly on the comb and ion-control prizes and so score lower on originality. They use the comb, but the magic-wavelength lattice is not contained in either earlier prize, and the many-atom regime is the part that is new. I agree with him that the committee should not construct a hybrid of B023 and B040 or drop a name from B038 to make room for a second part. If the vote goes to B038 I will support it, because his three-name configuration and citation wording are the cleanest available.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct achievement or as the third prize in a frequency-metrology sequence after 2005 and 2012; I cannot settle that by argument and it is the crux of my position.

The lattice-clock priority history beyond Katori and Ye, and the details of the gravitational-redshift and many-body-interaction results I cite from memory, are not verified against a supplied source.
Whether my past Hall-laboratory link should lead me to recuse on B045, which would leave Lindroth as the only supporter and make B038 the effective choice.

Whether B038 is mature enough: I now regard the pairing mechanism as a weaker objection than I did in round 1, but I remain uncertain how the committee will treat the first-author and other-group credit.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged in substance. My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Ye's work is closely tied to Hall's group at JILA; the profile documents no direct collaboration, co-authorship or supervision relationship with Katori or Ye, and I am not asserting one. On B045 I will disclose this link and I am willing to recuse from the final ballot on that candidate if the committee thinks that is right, in which case my preference should not be counted as support for B045. I am also an atomic and quantum-optics physicist whose Lund quantum-memory and quantum-information work lies near B007 and B028 without involving the credited names, as far as the profile shows. I have no documented conflict on B038.
